It usually sounds like this. You believe nothing came from something. Or science claims that we all came from soup, or maybe even science says that we all came from monkeys. These statements are presented as if they are summaries of scientific belief. They are not. They're not scientific positions, scientific conclusions, or scientific theories. They are caricatures, simplified distortions created by critics, not claims put forward by scientists. What's important to understand here is that in nearly 100% of cases, no scientist has ever made these claims. You will not find them in textbooks, peer-reviewed papers, or serious scientific explanations of cosmology or evolution. These ideas are not being argued against because they were never argued for in the first place. So where do they come from? They come from assumptions projected onto science, often by people who either do not understand the theories they're criticizing or who need those theories to sound absurd in order to protect something else. Turning a complex, carefully defined scientific model into a cartoon makes it easier to dismiss without engaging its actual content. This is why calling this a disagreement is misleading. Disagreement requires two sides addressing the same claim. What's happening here isn't engagement, it's substitution. Instead of responding to what science actually says, critics swap it out for a weaker, more ridiculous version. They argue against that instead. And because the replacement is easier to knock down, it creates the illusion of victory without ever touching the real argument. Once you recognize this move, it becomes hard to unsee. You start noticing how often science is not being debated, but impersonated, misrepresented in order to be defeated. And that realization alone should make us pause before taking most science versus religion arguments at face value.
